```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

# How to use this guide

- **Do Parts 1–4 once.** They take about 20–30 minutes total.
- **Part 5 is the routine** you'll repeat every time you work on the project.
- Copy each code chunk into the **R Console** (bottom-left pane in RStudio) and press Enter. Do not paste it into the proposal file.
- If something goes wrong, check **Part 8: When things go wrong** before panicking. Almost every mistake in Git can be undone.

**Our repo:** <https://github.com/Blockmg/STAT574MesquiteandGrass>

## The big idea in 30 seconds

Think of the GitHub repo as the **shared master copy** of the project. Each of us has our **own copy** on our laptop.

| Word | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Pull** | Download teammates' latest changes to your Computer |
| **Commit** | Save a labelled snapshot of your changes (on your computer only) |
| **Push** | Upload your commits to GitHub |
| **Branch** | A private copy of the project where you can work without affecting anyone else |
| **Pull request (PR)** | A request to merge your branch into the shared `main` version, so teammates can look first |

The rhythm is: **Pull → work on a branch → Commit → Push → Pull request → Merge.**

---

# Part 1: Install the tools (once)

## 1.1 Install Git

- **Windows:** download Git from <https://gitforwindows.org> and click through the installer, keeping all the default options.
- **Mac:** open the Terminal app, type `xcode-select --install`, and press Enter. Accept the prompt.

Then **close and reopen RStudio**.

## 1.2 Check that RStudio sees Git

In RStudio go to **Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN**. The box labelled *Git executable* should show a path (something like `C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe` or `/usr/bin/git`). If it's empty, restart your computer and check again.

## 1.3 Install the helper packages

```{r}
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds", "here"))
```

---

# Part 2: Connect R to your GitHub account (once)

You need a GitHub account first. Make one at <https://github.com> if you don't have one, and send your username to Maiya so she can add you (Part 3).

## 2.1 Tell Git who you are

Use the **same email** that's on your GitHub account, so your work shows up under your name.

```{r}
usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@arizona.edu"
)
```

## 2.2 Create a GitHub "token" (a password for R)

GitHub doesn't accept your regular password from R. Instead you make a token.

```{r}
usethis::create_github_token()
```

A GitHub page opens in your browser with the right boxes already ticked.

1. Under *Expiration*, pick a date **after the end of the semester**.
2. Scroll down and click **Generate token**.
3. **Copy the token** (it starts with `ghp_`). You won't be able to see it again.

Now give it to R:

```{r}
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Paste the token when asked and press Enter.

## 2.3 Check that everything worked

```{r}
usethis::git_sitrep()
```

Look for your name, your email, and a line saying your token is valid. If you see red ✖ marks, see Part 8.

---

# Part 3: Get access to the repo (once)

**Maiya (the repo owner)** does this for everyone else:

1. Open the repo on GitHub and click **Settings** (top bar).
2. Click **Collaborators** in the left menu, then **Add people**.
3. Enter each teammate's GitHub username.

**Everyone else:** check your email for the invitation and click **Accept**. You can't push anything until you accept.

---

# Part 4: Download the project to your laptop (once)

Pick a sensible folder, such as `Documents/STAT574`. Avoid cloud-synced folders like OneDrive, Dropbox, or iCloud, because they can fight with Git.

```{r}
usethis::create_from_github(
  "Blockmg/STAT574MesquiteandGrass",
  destdir = "~/Documents/STAT574",
  fork    = FALSE
)
```

RStudio opens the project in a new window. You should now see:

- A **Git** tab in the top-right pane (next to Environment and History).
- The project name `STAT574MesquiteandGrass` in the top-right corner of RStudio.
- The `Script/` folder with the proposal in the Files pane.

**From now on, always open the project by double-clicking `STAT574MesquiteandGrass.Rproj`** (or using the project menu in the top-right corner). If you open the `.Rmd` file directly, the Git tab won't appear.

**Alternative without code:** File → New Project → Version Control → Git, then paste `https://github.com/Blockmg/STAT574MesquiteandGrass.git` as the repository URL.

# Part 5: The everyday routine

Do this every time you sit down to work.

## 5.1 Pull first

In the **Git tab**, click the **blue down arrow (Pull)**. This grabs anything teammates have added since last time.

> **Make this a habit.** Most problems come from working on an old copy.

## 5.2 Make a branch for your task

Click the **purple branch icon (New Branch)** in the Git tab. Give it a short name that says what you're doing, for example:

- `rq1-random-forest`
- `rq2-glm-model`
- `proposal-responsibilities-table`
- `fix-typos-intro`

Leave *Sync branch with remote* ticked and click **Create**. The branch name now shows in the top-right of the Git tab. That's how you know which branch you're on.

## 5.3 Do your work

Edit files, write code, knit, and save as normal. Files you change will appear in the Git tab with a status letter:

| Letter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M** (blue) | Modified |
| **?** (yellow) | New file Git hasn't seen before |
| **D** (red) | Deleted |

## 5.4 Commit (save a snapshot)

1. Click **Commit** in the Git tab. A new window opens.
2. **Tick the boxes** next to the files you want to include. The bottom half shows exactly what changed: green lines were added, red lines were removed.
3. Write a short message in the top-right box saying **what you did**:
   - Good: `Add random forest training code for RQ1`
   - Good: `Fill in Person B responsibilities`
   - Not helpful: `update`, `stuff`, `asdf`
4. Click **Commit**, then close the pop-up.

Commit whenever you finish a small piece of work. Several small commits are better than one huge one.

## 5.5 Push (upload)

Click the **green up arrow (Push)**. Your branch and commits are now on GitHub, but `main` hasn't changed yet.

## 5.6 Open a pull request

1. Go to the repo on GitHub. A yellow banner appears: **"your-branch had recent pushes"**. Click **Compare & pull request**.
2. Write a sentence or two about what you changed and anything you'd like feedback on.
3. On the right, add a teammate under **Reviewers**.
4. Click **Create pull request**.

## 5.7 Review and merge

- **Reviewer:** open the PR, click the **Files changed** tab, and look over the changes. Leave comments if needed, then click **Merge pull request → Confirm merge**.
- **Author:** after it's merged, click **Delete branch** on GitHub.

## 5.8 Go back to `main`

In RStudio's Git tab, use the **branch dropdown** (top-right of the tab) to switch back to `main`, then click **Pull**. You're now up to date and ready to start the next task at step 5.2.

# Part 6: Rules that keep us out of trouble

## Don't put the drone or lidar data on GitHub

GitHub **rejects any file over 100 MB**, and the orthomosaics, lidar point clouds, and canopy height models will be much bigger than that. Once a huge file is committed, it's painful to remove.

- Keep raw data in a **shared drive** (Box, Google Drive, etc.). *We should probably make one of those or if Lindsey has a folder she wants to share we can use that.*
- Each person puts a copy in a `data/` folder inside the project on their own laptop.
- `data/` is listed in `.gitignore`, so Git never tries to upload it.
- Read files with `here::here()` so the paths work on everyone's laptop:

```{r}
library(here)
chm   <- terra::rast(here("data", "site1_chm.tif"))
flux  <- read.csv(here("data", "flux_daily.csv"))
```

Never use a path like `C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/...`; it only works on your machine.

Small things are fine to commit: scripts, the `.Rmd` files, small summary tables (under a few MB), and figures for the report.

## Other rules

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **Pull before you start** | You build on the latest version |
| **Never work directly on `main`** | Everything gets checked before it's shared |
| **One branch per task** | Easy to see who's doing what |
| **Stick to your own files/sections when possible** | Fewer conflicts (see Part 7) |
| **Don't commit knitted `.html` files** | Everyone's knit is slightly different and causes fake conflicts |
| **Push at least once per work session** | Your work is backed up and teammates can see progress |

---

# Part 7: Splitting the work so we don't collide

Right now the whole proposal is one file. That's fine for the proposal. For the **report**, it will help to give each research question its own file, matching the responsibilities table:

```
Script/
  report.Rmd            <- main file that pulls the pieces together
  01-intro-data.Rmd     <- Person D
  02-methods.Rmd        <- Person A
  03-rq1-results.Rmd    <- Person A
  04-rq2-results.Rmd    <- Person B
  05-rq3-results.Rmd    <- Person C
  06-conclusions.Rmd
R/
  rq1_random_forest.R
  rq2_glm.R
  rq3_fpca.R
```

Inside `report.Rmd`, each piece is pulled in with an empty "child" chunk. Type three backticks, then `{r child = "03-rq1-results.Rmd"}`, and on the next line close the chunk with three backticks. Knitting `report.Rmd` then drops each section's text and code in at that spot, in order.

When people work in **different files**, Git combines their work automatically.

Two other habits help a lot:

- **Write one sentence per line** in the text parts of `.Rmd` files. It looks odd, but it makes changes much easier to compare and merge. Line breaks within a paragraph don't show up in the knitted document.
- **Don't reformat text you didn't change** (re-wrapping paragraphs, re-indenting code). It shows up as a change and can create conflicts.

# Part 8: When things go wrong

## "Merge conflict"

This means you and a teammate changed the **same lines** of the same file. Git can't guess which version to keep, so it marks the spot:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your version of the sentence.
=======
Your teammate's version of the sentence.
>>>>>>> main
```

To fix it:

1. Open the file and find the `<<<<<<<` markers. The Git tab shows the file with an orange **U**.
2. Edit the text so it says what it **should** say. Keep one version, combine them, or rewrite.
3. **Delete all three marker lines** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`).
4. Save, then Commit (tick the file) and Push.

If you're not sure which version is right, text the teammate. It usually takes a minute to sort out.

## "Push rejected" / "Updates were rejected"

Someone pushed to the same branch before you. Click **Pull** first, then **Push** again.

## I made changes on `main` by accident

If you haven't committed yet, just create a new branch now (step 5.2). Your uncommitted changes come with you to the new branch.

If you already committed to `main` but haven't pushed, ask Brandon or another teammate for help before pushing.

## The Git tab disappeared

You probably opened the `.Rmd` file without opening the project. Open `STAT574MesquiteandGrass.Rproj`.

## Authentication failed / asked for a password

Your token expired or wasn't saved. Redo step 2.2, then run `usethis::git_sitrep()`.

## I want to throw away my changes to a file and start over

In the Git tab, right-click the file → **Revert**. This resets it to the last commit. **This can't be undone**, so be sure.

## I want to see an older version of something

Click the **clock icon (History)** in the Git tab. You can see every commit, who made it, and exactly what changed. On GitHub, open any file and click **History** or **Blame** (who last changed each line).

---

# Part 9: Tracking who's doing what (GitHub Issues)

Use **Issues** on GitHub as our shared to-do list. It keeps everything in one place instead of scattered across texts.

1. Go to the **Issues** tab of the repo → **New issue**.
2. Give it a clear title, e.g. *"Hand-label reference points for Site 1"*.
3. On the right, **assign** it to whoever is doing it.
4. When you open a pull request that finishes the task, write `Closes #7` (using the issue's number) in the description. The issue closes automatically when the PR is merged.

**Optional:** the **Projects** tab can turn the issues into a board with columns like *To do → In progress → Done*.

---

# Part 10: Your first practice run

Try the whole routine once on something small and low-risk before doing real work.

1. Open the project and **Pull**.
2. Create a branch called `practice-yourname`.
3. Open `Script/Stat574 Final Project Proposal.Rmd`. In the **Group Member Responsibilities** section, under the table, add one line:
   `- Your Name: confirmed I can push to GitHub`
4. Save, **Commit** with the message `Practice commit from Your Name`, and **Push**.
5. Open a **pull request** on GitHub and request a review from one teammate.
6. Review someone else's practice PR and merge it.
7. Switch back to `main` and **Pull**. You should see everyone's practice lines.

If all four lines show up, the team is set up correctly.

# Quick reference card

| I want to... | Do this |
|---|---|
| Get teammates' latest work | Git tab → **Pull** (blue ↓) |
| Start a new task | Git tab → **New Branch** (purple icon) |
| Save a snapshot | Git tab → **Commit** → tick files → message → Commit |
| Upload my work | Git tab → **Push** (green ↑) |
| Ask to merge my work | GitHub → **Compare & pull request** |
| See which branch I'm on | Top-right of the Git tab |
| Switch branches | Branch dropdown in the Git tab |
| See history | Git tab → **clock icon** |
| Check my setup | `usethis::git_sitrep()` |

**More help:** *Happy Git and GitHub for the useR* by Jenny Bryan, free at <https://happygitwithr.com>.
